Sweetest Dew Old Tree Heirloom White (Watermelon White)

August 12, 2026August 23, 2026 Post a comment
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:37
Instaread

Country of Origin: China
Leaf Appearance: huge, mixed green and brown
Water Temperature: 212 degrees
Steep Time: 30 seconds
Preparation Method:  porcelain gaiwan
Liquor: amber

I first met Dylan from Sweetest Dew when he was a customer at a tea shop I worked at years ago. He has since moved to China to learn about tea. It’s been a lot of fun to follow his journey, especially the videos he shares on Instagram. Dylan sources some really interesting teas, and I finally got around to placing an order. The Watermelon White is one that I’ve heard a lot about from tea friends. It was definitely the first to get added to my cart.

Tea
blogging
Blogging Resources & Services

Leaf

Sweetest Dew Old Tree Heirloom White (Watermelon White) was made from 200-year-old trees in Zhe Rong. The leaves were unshaped and absolutely huge. They were somewhat broken, with several long stems still attached. It took some doing just to get 5g of this tea into my biggest porcelain gaiwan. My first infusion had a steep time of 30 seconds, and that was gradually increased with each round.

Liquor

Sweetest Dew Old Tree Heirloom White (Watermelon White) brewed up a gold liquor. The taste was very sweet with a crisp and clean finish. It almost reminded me of Riesling wine in that way. There was a vegetal character that was definitely reminiscent of watermelon rind. It was juicy yet tart at the same time with a lingering aftertaste that lasted long after each sip. It had a thick mouthfeel that became even more prominent once the tea cooled. This is a tea that just keeps going and going. I had 6+ infusions, and the leaves are barely softened.

I will usually brew with fully boiling water when evaluating a tea, unless the retailer instructs otherwise. I decided to give this tea another try with 175℉ water since some people recommended treating white tea a little more gently. The result was a gentler version, but the watermelon notes were still there. I do think I prefer the intensity that hotter water brings out. This tea never really gets bitter or astringent. Don’t be afraid to push it a little more.

Have you ever tried Sweetest Dew Old Tree Heirloom White (Watermelon White)? Let me know your thoughts on this tea in the comments below!
